title: Timing-Dependent Effects of Melatonin Supplementation on Athletic Performance and Exercise-Induced Muscle Damage: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
content: Background: Optimizing athletic performance while mitigat-ing exercise-induced stress remains a persistent challenge in sports science. Melatonin, an endogenous neurohormone with dual chronobiotic and antioxidant properties, offers unique therapeutic potential. This study provides the first compre-hensive, timing- and dose-stratified evaluation of melatonin's effects on athletic performance and exercise-induced tissue damage. Methods: We searched PubMed, Web of Science, SPORTDis-cus, and Cochrane Library through September 2025 for ran-domized controlled trials examining melatonin supplementa-tion versus placebo on athletic performance and muscle damage biomarkers. Results: Nineteen trials involving 266 participants were in-cluded. Melatonin supplementation significantly improved athletic performance and reduced muscle damage biomarkers through timing-dependent mechanisms. High-certainty evi-dence supports moderate effects for endurance performance and small effects for explosive power. Evening administration with administration-to-exercise intervals exceeding six hours produced optimal benefits, while daytime administration showed negligible effects. Multi-day supplementation demon-strated substantially greater efficacy than acute dosing. However, significant publication bias was detected for muscle damage outcomes, and evidence for strength, coordination, and speed performance remains inconclusive. Conclusions: High-certainty evidence demonstrates that melatonin supplementation enhances endurance performance and reduces exercise-induced muscle damage when adminis-tered in the evening with adequate timing intervals. Findings support implementing evidence-based melatonin supplemen-tation for endurance athletes during intensive training peri-ods, while recognizing uncertain benefits for strength and power activities.
